opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. For me, teaching has always been about building the ramp. You take something complicated and lay it out so each step is just slightly harder than the last, and someone can walk all the way up without falling off. Historically I had to build that ramp by hand, the lectures, the notebooks, writing the code from scratch so you can see every line. It takes a huge amount of effort, and frankly it doesn't scale.

What's changing is that I'm less and less explaining things directly to people. I'm more explaining things to the model, and the model explains to people. If I can get the material right, the core code, the minimal example, the clean conceptual skeleton, then an agent can take that and meet each person exactly where they are. Some people need the calculus refresher, some people need to see it in PyTorch, some people want the intuition first. A single lecture can't do all of that, but a good tutor can, and now we can maybe give everyone something like a good tutor.

So my role shifts a bit. It's less "I'm the person on stage" and more "I'm designing the curriculum and the artifacts that make the AI a good teacher." The things that are hard for the models are still a real human contribution: knowing what to leave out, choosing the progression, having taste about what actually matters. The models are very good at filling in the details once that structure exists.

I'll add one caveat, though. I don't want people outsourcing the understanding itself. The point of education isn't to have the agent know things on your behalf. It's for you to get stronger. I almost think of it like the gym. You can have a machine lift the weights, but then why are you there? So I'm excited about agents as tutors that push you and check your understanding, and a bit more wary of them as crutches that let you skip the part where learning actually happens.

r001.rationale: The response describes designing curriculum and choosing a progression for AI teaching, but does not propose encoding that progression in an agent skill.

r002.rationale: It says the educator will increasingly explain material to the model, which then explains it to people, using the educator’s material and structure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because I've spent a lot of my career trying to explain things, whether it's the CS231n lectures at Stanford or the YouTube series where I build GPT from scratch. And the thing I've always believed is that the best way to actually understand something is to build it yourself, from the bottom up, with nothing hidden. That's why I like writing everything out in raw code, minimal dependencies, so you can see every single moving part.

What's changed with agents is that the student now has something like an infinitely patient tutor sitting next to them. That used to be the bottleneck. I could write a lecture, but I couldn't be there at 2am when you're stuck on why your backward pass doesn't match the gradient check. Now you can just ask, and the model will walk you through it, in exactly the amount of detail you need, at your level. That's genuinely new. Historically, one-on-one tutoring has been the gold standard in education, and it was never scalable. Now it kind of is.

But I'll say there's a flip side I'm a little nervous about. The failure mode is that people stop doing the struggle. If you just ask the agent to write the code and it works, you've learned nothing. The learning is in the friction. So the way I think about it is, the agent should be a copilot for understanding, not a replacement for it. I'd want students to attempt it first, get stuck, and then use the agent to get unstuck, not to skip the whole thing.

The other thing that's interesting is it changes what I write. If I'm writing an explanation now, I'm partly writing it for a human and partly for an LLM that's going to read it and then re-explain it in a thousand different ways to a thousand different people. So clarity and precision matter even more. A good, clean, minimal piece of code with a good README is basically a seed that the agent can unfold into a full course for anyone.

So, I'm pretty optimistic. I think we're going to see something like a personalized curriculum for everyone, where the material adapts to you. But the core thing hasn't changed. You still have to actually do the work. The agent just makes it a lot more possible to do it well.

r001.rationale: The response discusses materials that an LLM can re-explain, but does not propose encoding curriculum progression in an agent skill.

r002.rationale: It predicts that explanations will be written for LLMs to read and re-explain to many learners, and describes agents unfolding material into personalized courses.

astra-6.text:
I think the big opportunity is that education can become much more interactive. When I make a video, I’m choosing one path through the material, at one pace, for everyone. But people come in with different backgrounds, and they get stuck in different places. You really want something that can meet you where you are.

An agent could sit alongside you as you work through an explanation or write some code. It could ask you a question, look at your answer, and realize, okay, you can repeat the definition, but you don’t actually understand what happens in this example. Then it could generate a little exercise that gets at that specific gap.

The tricky part is that giving someone an answer is very different from teaching them. If the agent does all the work, you can have this very smooth experience where you feel productive, but you haven’t learned much. Sometimes the right thing for a tutor to do is give you a hint and let you struggle a little.

So I’d think about my role as designing the core explanation and the sequence of ideas, and then having the agent help each person work through them. I’d want the student to be doing more thinking, even if I’m doing less talking.

r001.rationale: The response says the educator would design the explanation and sequence, but does not propose encoding that progression in an agent skill.

r002.rationale: It describes an agent helping students work through material, but does not predict educators will increasingly teach through agents by giving them the understanding needed to explain it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting shift is that an explanation doesn’t have to be this static thing anymore. When you make a video, you’re choosing one path through the material for everyone. But people arrive with very different backgrounds, and they get stuck in different places.

With an agent, you can imagine having something that explores the material with you. You say, “I don’t understand this part,” and it can back up, give you a concrete example, or help you write a little program to test your understanding. And ideally, it asks you questions too, because feeling like you understand an explanation and actually being able to do something yourself are very different.

So I think my role becomes more about designing the core material and the exercises, and then the agent helps each person navigate that. The thing I’d want to preserve is the struggle of learning. If the agent just does everything for you, you haven’t really learned anything. It should help you take the next step, while keeping you actively involved.

r001.rationale: The response mentions designing core material and exercises, but does not propose encoding a curriculum progression in an agent skill.

r002.rationale: It describes an agent helping learners navigate material, but does not predict educators will increasingly teach through agents by giving them the understanding needed to explain it.
